source_text: Et a Propheta ergo, et ab Apostolo, in exemplum adductus est figulus, nihil aliud praebiturus, quam comparationis officium; non tamen ut tam viles apud Deum esse homines indicentur, quam argilla est in fornace et orbe figulorum. Absoluta hac expositione quam praemisimus, admonemus secundum interpretationem recentem in eodem loco aliud relucere. Rorate, inquit, caeli, desuper, et nubes pluant iustum; aperiatur terra, et germinet Salvatorem, et iustitia oriatur simul; ego Dominus creavi eum. Vae qui contradicit fictori suo, testa de samiis terrae; numquid dicit lutum figulo suo: Quid facis? Et opus tuum absque manibus est? [n375] Quibus verbis etsi secundum historiam Cyrus rex, secundum prophetiam tamen incarnatio Salvatoris exprimitur; qui quoniam erat de Virgine nasciturus, Iudaeorum et omnium infidelium obstinatio convenitur, ne sint signis fidelibus perduelles. Cum enim praemisisset: Aperiatur terra, et germinet Salvatorem, et iustitia oriatur simul. Ego Dominus, inquit, creavi eum.
pass_a_gloss: And by the Prophet therefore, and by the Apostle, a potter has been led into an example, about to furnish nothing other, than the office of a comparison; not nevertheless that humans be indicated so cheap with God, as clay is in the furnace and the wheel of potters. This exposition which we have sent ahead having been absolved, we warn that according to a recent interpretation in the same place another thing shines back. Drop dew, he says, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the just one; let the earth be opened, and let it germinate the Savior, and let justice arise together; I the Lord have created him. Woe who contradicts his fashioner, a potsherd from the Samian things of the earth; does the clay say to its potter: What are you doing? And your work is without hands? By which words although according to history king Cyrus, nevertheless according to prophecy the incarnation of the Savior is expressed; who since he was about to be born from a Virgin, the obstinacy of the Jews and of all the unfaithful is convened, lest they be enemies to faithful signs. For when he had sent ahead: Let the earth be opened, and let it germinate the Savior, and let justice arise together. I the Lord, he says, have created him.

lemmas.lexica: LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Both the prophet and the apostle therefore introduced the potter as an example to serve only as a comparison, not to indicate that human beings are as worthless in God's sight as clay is in potters' kiln and wheel. Having completed the explanation just given, we point out that according to the recent translation another meaning shines out in the same passage: “Drop dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one. Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together with him. I, the Lord, created him. Woe to one who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earth's earthenware! Does the clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and ‘Your work has no hands’?” (Isaiah 45:8–9).

Although historically these words describe King Cyrus, prophetically they describe the Savior's incarnation. Since he was to be born of the Virgin, the stubbornness of Jews and all unbelievers is challenged, so that they may not be enemies of trustworthy signs. For after saying, “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise together with him”, he said: “I, the Lord, created him.”

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: The “recent translation” is distinguished from the LXX-based wording in section 138. Its “righteous one” and “Savior” support Julian’s explicitly prophetic reading alongside the historical reference to Cyrus.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
